power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: This systematic review examined current findings on implicit statistical learning (ISL) in schizophrenia spectrum disorders and the factors that influence performance.
We aimed to update and expand the existing literature by including various ISL tasks, such as serial reaction time, artificial grammar learning, or transitional probabilities.
We also considered several ISL moderators related to the characteristics of these tasks, as well as a host of potential clinical and cognitive correlates.
We searched PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO, and MEDLINE Complete for original studies published in English involving adults diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
Twenty-one studies published between 1992 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria.
We extracted relevant data including study information and design, sample characteristics, ISL task type and characteristics, and main outcomes.
Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Assessment Scale.
Findings were heterogeneous, with studies reporting both intact and impaired ISL.
The most frequently reported outcome with the largest aggregate patient sample showed that ISL was preserved in comparison to healthy controls.
Seven studies reported ISL deficits, and the rest reported mixed or condition-specific findings.
The most promising moderators included task and stimulus type.
Disorganized symptomatology and working memory span consistently correlated with ISL performance.
In contrast, antipsychotic dosage, overall symptomatology, illness duration, or explicit memory did not show consistent associations with ISL.
Implicit statistical learning (ISL) describes our ability to learn the rules of patterned stimuli in the environment (Christiansen, 2019).
text.formatted: Implicit statistical learning (ISL) describes our ability to learn the rules of patterned stimuli in the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Christiansen, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The term "statistical learning" was originally introduced by (Saffran et al., 1996) emphasizing the importance of experience-independent mechanisms in language acquisition.
text.formatted: The term "statistical learning" was originally introduced by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Saffran et al., 1996)</ref> emphasizing the importance of experience-independent mechanisms in language acquisition.

text.text: Their study showed that 8-month-old infants can segment words from fluent speech based solely on statistical relationships between neighboring speech sounds.
In 2006, the authors of an artificial grammar learning experiment adopted the term ISL (Conway & Christiansen, 2006).
text.formatted: In 2006, the authors of an artificial grammar learning experiment adopted the term ISL <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Conway & Christiansen, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: They stated that ISL refers to the ability to automatically detect and internalize statistical patterns and regularities in environmental input without deliberate effort.

ISL is typically measured using behavioral experimental paradigms that expose participants to structured sequences of stimuli and later test whether they have become sensitive to the statistical regularities embedded in those sequences.

These paradigms usually involve an incidental exposure phase followed by an indirect test of learning such as reaction time differences, familiarity judgments, or prediction tasks (Jenkins et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These paradigms usually involve an incidental exposure phase followed by an indirect test of learning such as reaction time differences, familiarity judgments, or prediction tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jenkins et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: One of the most widely used methods is the Serial Reaction Time (SRT) task, where participants view a neutral target stimulus that appears at one of four locations and are required to quickly and accurately press the key that corresponds spatially to the location of the stimulus (Adini et al., 2015; Green et al., 1997).
text.formatted: One of the most widely used methods is the Serial Reaction Time (SRT) task, where participants view a neutral target stimulus that appears at one of four locations and are required to quickly and accurately press the key that corresponds spatially to the location of the stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Adini et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Green et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Without the participants' knowledge, the stimulus location is altered in successive trials according to a fixed underlying sequence, which should slow the response time.
The reaction time difference between sequence and random trials measures implicit sequence learning.
In probabilistic paradigms, random stimuli are presented throughout the entire test rather than at the end (Horan et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In probabilistic paradigms, random stimuli are presented throughout the entire test rather than at the end <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Horan et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Other ISL tasks in common use include artificial grammar learning or transitional probabilities tasks; these tend to include passive exposure phases succeeded by a reflectionbased test phase.

The artificial grammar learning task, for example, first presents participants with many sequences of stimuli that, unbeknownst to them, conform to certain rules and thus contain predictable statistical regularities.

During the testing phase, participants are presented with some sequences that follow the same rules as the learning sequences (grammatical sequences) and some sequences that violate them (ungrammatical sequences).

Different responses to grammatical sequences compared to ungrammatical ones can serve as evidence that the participant learned at least some rules or statistical regularities (Danion et al., 2001; Hsieh et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Different responses to grammatical sequences compared to ungrammatical ones can serve as evidence that the participant learned at least some rules or statistical regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Danion et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hsieh et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, ISL is likely not a unitary ability; correlations among ISL tasks tend to be low (Gebauer & Mackintosh, 2007) and performance may further depend on factors like the sensory modality or type of utilized stimuli (Christiansen, 2019; Siegelman & Frost, 2015).
text.formatted: Importantly, ISL is likely not a unitary ability; correlations among ISL tasks tend to be low <ref type="bibr">(Gebauer & Mackintosh, 2007)</ref> and performance may further depend on factors like the sensory modality or type of utilized stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Christiansen, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: One of the central issues in ISL research has been the distinction between implicit and explicit learning.

This was first prominently established in the context of amnesia, where patients with severe deficits in explicit (declarative) memory demonstrated a relatively preserved capacity to acquire new skills and habits implicitly (Cohen & Squire, 1980).
text.formatted: This was first prominently established in the context of amnesia, where patients with severe deficits in explicit (declarative) memory demonstrated a relatively preserved capacity to acquire new skills and habits implicitly <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cohen & Squire, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: This dissociation supported the view that implicit and explicit memory are subserved by at least partially separable systems (Amodio, 2025).
text.formatted: This dissociation supported the view that implicit and explicit memory are subserved by at least partially separable systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Amodio, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In clinical populations, ISL tasks offer a way to test whether procedural, rule-based, or sequence learning remains intact despite deficits in explicit memory.
In the psychiatric population, research on ISL initially focused on schizophrenia, where early studies using the SRT task suggested alterations in ISL (Green et al., 1997).
text.formatted: In the psychiatric population, research on ISL initially focused on schizophrenia, where early studies using the SRT task suggested alterations in ISL <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Green et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Subsequent research extended these paradigms to other clinical populations, including developmental disorders such as dyslexia and autism (Bell et al., 2025), as well as ADHD (Richards et al., 2020; Rosas et al., 2010) and mood disorders (Pedersen et al., 2009), with mixed findings.
text.formatted: Subsequent research extended these paradigms to other clinical populations, including developmental disorders such as dyslexia and autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bell et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as ADHD <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Richards et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Rosas et al., 2010)</ref> and mood disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Pedersen et al., 2009)</ref>, with mixed findings.

text.text: In schizophrenia spectrum disorders, patients often show robust and consistent deficits in explicit learning (Cornelis et al., 2022; Geana et al., 2022) and memory (Aleman et al., 1999; Cirillo & Seidman, 2003; Hannaoui et al., 2025), whereas their performance on implicit tasks seems to be more variable (Danion et al., 2001; Horan et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In schizophrenia spectrum disorders, patients often show robust and consistent deficits in explicit learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cornelis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Geana et al., 2022)</ref> and memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aleman et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cirillo & Seidman, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hannaoui et al., 2025)</ref>, whereas their performance on implicit tasks seems to be more variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Danion et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Horan et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: It has been suggested that intact aspects of implicit learning may partly explain why, despite explicit memory deficits, many patients retain a degree of everyday functional competence, since abilities such as recognizing typical patterns of social interaction or the pragmatics of language are thought to be learned largely automatically (Danion et al., 2001; Horan et al., 2008).
text.formatted: It has been suggested that intact aspects of implicit learning may partly explain why, despite explicit memory deficits, many patients retain a degree of everyday functional competence, since abilities such as recognizing typical patterns of social interaction or the pragmatics of language are thought to be learned largely automatically <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Danion et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Horan et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, impaired ISL could contribute to difficulties in social and functional domains that rely on automatically acquired knowledge (Couture, 2006).
text.formatted: Conversely, impaired ISL could contribute to difficulties in social and functional domains that rely on automatically acquired knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Couture, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: However, direct evidence linking ISL performance to functional or social outcomes remains limited and inconsistent; at least one study found no significant association between implicit learning and social or rehabilitation outcomes in schizophrenia (Woonings et al., 2003).

text.text: The main aim of this systematic review was to examine the current data on ISL in schizophrenia spectrum disorders and the factors which influence the performance.
To the best of our knowledge, the latest systematic review and meta-analysis on ISL in this population focused only on the SRT task, including studies published by 2006 (Siegert et al., 2008).
text.formatted: To the best of our knowledge, the latest systematic review and meta-analysis on ISL in this population focused only on the SRT task, including studies published by 2006 <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Siegert et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Our goal was to update this information and to expand it to other tasks such as artificial grammar learning or transitional probabilities.
We also sought to consider potential moderating factors related to ISL task characteristics, as in the sensory modality and other characteristics of the utilized stimuli.
Of clinical factors, we considered symptomatology, illness duration and phase, and medication.
Finally, we probed potential cognitive correlates, particularly in working memory and other explicit memory systems.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: We searched four main databases: Pubmed, SCOPUS, PsycINFO and Medline Complete with the keywords schizo* OR psychotic OR psychosis and "statistical learning" OR "implicit learning" in combination.
We supplemented the database search by reviewing the reference lists of articles meeting our inclusion criteria (backward reference search).

The inclusion criteria were 1) original research studies, 2) written in English, and 3) participants were adults diagnosed with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder based on the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) or The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) criteria.
We excluded reviews and meta-analyses as well as studies where participants had a known history of neurological disorders or dual psychiatric diagnoses.

Articles resulting from the initial database searches were imported into the Covidence software (Veritas Health Innovation Ltd, Melbourne, Australia), where duplicate records were removed and studies were further screened.
Two researchers performed this task (KK and MV) and, in case of disagreement, a third independent researcher (BK) evaluated the study.
Full copies of articles identified by the search were obtained for data synthesis.
A flowchart of the selection process is presented in Figure 1, following PRISMA guidelines.
text.formatted: A flowchart of the selection process is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, following PRISMA guidelines.

text.text: The review protocol was registered with PROSPERO (Registration number: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251051011).
text.formatted: The review protocol was registered with PROSPERO (Registration number: <ref type="url" target="https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251051011">CRD420251051011</ref>).

text.text: Study quality and risk of bias were assessed according to the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for observational studies by two independent reviewers (MV and BK).

The NOS evaluates methodological quality across three broad domains: (1) selection of study groups, (2) comparability of groups, and (3) ascertainment of exposure or outcome, depending on the study design.

Within these domains, studies are awarded a series of points (or "stars") based on predefined criteria, such as the representativeness of the sample, adequacy of control selection, adjustment for confounding variables, and the reliability of outcome or exposure assessment.
Higher scores indicate better methodological quality and lower risk of bias.
The quality score of a given study was based on a score of six as a cut-off point to distinguish high from low quality studies.

We extracted the following data from the selected articles: study information (authors, year, country, and design), sample characteristics (number of participants, sex, age, education, diagnosis, and control group), ISL task type and characteristics, and main outcomes.
Where available, we also extracted information about the clinical characteristics of the patient group, including in illness duration and phase, medication, and symptomatology.
Cognitive correlates of interest included working memory and explicit memory..
The findings are presented as a narrative analysis and all studies selected from the database searches were summarized in table form and organized in alphabetical order.
Initially, we identified 169 studies (69 Scopus, 58 PubMed, 34 PsycINFO and 8 MEDLINE), of which 72 were identified as duplicates.
Of the 97 studies that were further screened, we included 21, all published between 1992 and 2025 (Figure 1).

text.text: Across the selection domain, case definition adequacy (Q1) and case representativeness (Q2) were virtually universal strengths across the majority of studies, supported by the consistent use of clinical diagnostic criteria and chart diagnoses.

Conversely, weaknesses in control selection and definition (Q3 and Q4) were particularly evident in lower-scoring studies, such as Orlov (2021), which earned the lowest score of 2 stars, and Green (1997), scoring 3 stars.

text.text: The most frequently used paradigm was the SRT task or its variants, which were employed in 13 (57%) of the 21 included studies.

Specifically, 12 studies used the standard SRT paradigm (Adini et al., 2015; Chrobak et al., 2017; Coman et al., 2010; Exner, Boucsein et al., 2006; Exner, Weniger et al., 2006; Green et al., 1997; Hinc et al., 2025; Marvel et al., 2005 Marvel et al., , 2007;; Pedersen et al., 2008; Reiss et al., 2006; Stevens et al., 2002), while one study used the Alternating SRT task (Schwartz et al., 2003).

text.text: Together, these sequence-learning paradigms accounted for nearly two thirds of the included studies, indicating a strong predominance of research on the implicit acquisition of sequential regularities.

Most studies that used SRT operationalized ISL as a sequence-specific reaction time effect, typically calculated as the difference in reaction times between sequenced and random task blocks or as the performance decrement following the introduction of a random sequence.

One study quantified ISL as the overall improvement in reaction time from the beginning to the end of training, reflecting general skill acquisition rather than sequencespecific learning (Coman et al., 2010).

text.text: Studies reporting preserved performance or mixed effects used a mix of ISL measures, including also the SRT task.

We noted a near-complete absence of investigations in the auditory or tactile domains, disallowing an assessment of sensory modality as a potential moderator of ISL performance in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.

Stimulus type did emerge as one of the moderators of ISL performance: two independently reported but methodologically similar studies from the same research group found a selective deficit for color-pattern material with relatively preserved learning of letter-string material (Chiu et al., 2005; Hsieh et al., 2004).

text.text: The main goal of this systematic review was to examine the current data on ISL in schizophrenia spectrum disorders and the factors that influence performance.
It extends the review of Siegert and colleagues from 2008 by including paradigms beyond the SRT and examining moderating factors of ISL performance and its clinical and cognitive correlates.
Our findings suggest heterogeneous outcomes as studies report both intact and impaired ISL in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
The most frequently reported outcome with the largest aggregate patient sample across studies showed that ISL was preserved in patients as compared to healthy controls.
Seven studies reported deficits in ISL and the rest reported mixed or condition-specific findings.
Most studies used visual and visual-motor paradigms to assess ISL.
Only one included study examined ISL across modalities using an audiovisual associative languagelearning task (Orlov et al., 2021).

text.text: This prevalence of visual paradigms may constrain the generalizability of available findings: ISL shows partial modality specificity in psychiatrically healthy samples, with early processing differences observed between the visual, auditory, and tactile domains (Christiansen, 2019; Siegelman & Frost, 2015).
text.formatted: This prevalence of visual paradigms may constrain the generalizability of available findings: ISL shows partial modality specificity in psychiatrically healthy samples, with early processing differences observed between the visual, auditory, and tactile domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Christiansen, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Future investigators may wish to examine potential modality-or stimulus-specific effects given also the extensive sensory processing deficits observed in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.

Impairments in early-stage visual processing, occurring as early as the retina and visual pathways, may destabilize the bottom-up visual signal needed for accurate perceptual representation (Adámek et al., 2022 (Adámek et al., , 2024)).

text.text: Auditory sensory processing shows a parallel pattern, where impaired basic auditory processes, such as tone matching, may contribute to overall cognitive deficits (Javitt & Sweet, 2015).
text.formatted: Auditory sensory processing shows a parallel pattern, where impaired basic auditory processes, such as tone matching, may contribute to overall cognitive deficits <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Javitt & Sweet, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The need to comprehensively examine the contribution of basic sensory processing is further underscored by a series of studies demonstrating a selective deficit for color-pattern material (Chiu et al., 2005; Hsieh et al., 2004).

text.text: The authors suggested that this deficit may be explained by early processes like sensory gating or perceptual priming, which may be more sensitive to the greater complexity of the color patterns compared with letter strings, for which learning was relatively preserved.
Of the reviewed studies, 57% used the SRT task or its variants to measure ISL.
Most operationalized ISL as a sequence-specific reaction time effect, with two studies by Marvel and colleagues (2005, 2007) considering also the proportion of correct responses across task blocks.
text.formatted: Most operationalized ISL as a sequence-specific reaction time effect, with two studies by <ref type="bibr">Marvel and</ref> <ref type="bibr">colleagues (2005, 2007)</ref> considering also the proportion of correct responses across task blocks.

text.text: The second most common approach, represented by 19% of the reviewed literature, used grammar-based paradigms like the artificial grammar learning task.
Among these, ISL was predominantly assessed using accuracy-based measures of grammatical classification.
Other ISL measures such as the transitional probabilities task were vastly under-represented, with only single instances across the reviewed studies.

While all SRT-based studies in this review required active, response-based engagement throughout, the grammar learning and perceptual paradigms also included passive exposure phases in which participants were typically instructed to observe stimuli before a subsequent active test phase.

Notably, all studies that reported impaired ISL performance in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders used some form of SRT tasks (Chrobak et al., 2017; Exner, Boucsein et al., 2006; Exner, Weniger et al., 2006; Green et al., 1997; Hinc et al., 2025; Pedersen et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Notably, all studies that reported impaired ISL performance in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders used some form of SRT tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chrobak et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Exner, Boucsein et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Exner, Weniger et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Green et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hinc et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pedersen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Schwartz et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: However, as no study varied exposure mode inside a single task type, it is not possible to determine whether active engagement itself might increase sensitivity to detecting an ISL deficit, or whether the SRT paradigms are simply more sensitive to sequence-learning impairment for other reasons such as their reliance on motor sequencing.
Additionally, Adini et al. (2015) and Marvel et al. (2007) both reported largely preserved performance using SRT, indicating that task type alone does not seem to fully determine the outcome.

text.text: It might be possible that other factors such as task duration, number of practice sessions, or particular demands of the sequence structure used within the SRT could impact the performance.

Lastly, a few studies have questioned the psychometric properties of the SRT paradigm itself suggesting poor testretest reliability (Oliveira et al., 2024) and construct validity (Trofimova et al., 2020) implying that the effect of the task may partly reflect rapid, temporary adaptation rather than ISL.

text.text: Besides ISL paradigms and engagement of the participants, we also examined the role of clinical characteristics in the performance.
Symptom severity showed a selective pattern across studies.

Rather than overall symptomatology, it was specifically disorganized symptoms that were repeatedly associated with poorer ISL performance (Chiu et al., 2005; Exner, Boucsein, et al., 2006), while positive and negative symptoms were largely unrelated to performance once other factors were accounted for (Adini et al., 2015; Marvel et al., 2005; Pedersen et al., 2008; Reiss et al., 2006; Schmand et al., 1992).

text.text: Illness phase and chronicity did not emerge as consistent moderators of ISL outcomes: impaired and preserved performance were reported in both first-episode and chronic samples (e.g., Pedersen et al., 2008; Green et al., 1997 vs. Coman et al., 2010; Valton et al., 2019).

text.text: The only study to follow the same patients over time suggested that clinical state, rather than illness duration, may be the more relevant factor, as ISL deficits present during an acute episode had largely resolved at a 20-month follow-up alongside a reduction in disorganized symptoms (Exner, Boucsein, et al., 2006).

text.text: Antipsychotic dosage also showed no relationship with ISL performance in any of the studies that examined it.

However, medication type may matter: in the one study that compared drug classes, patients treated with olanzapine performed comparably to healthy controls, whereas those on classic neuroleptics showed reduced ISL (Stevens et al., 2002).

text.text: A more reliable predictor of ISL performance seemed to be working memory.
Several studies found a significant association between a working memory task and ISL (Danion et al., 2001; Fernandez et al., 2021; Schwartz et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Several studies found a significant association between a working memory task and ISL <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Danion et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fernandez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Schwartz et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Working memory may be needed early in training as it does not seem to be related to the ultimate magnitude of ISL, but to the efficiency of the transition, meaning how quickly or reliably patients can enter an automatized mode of responding.

For instance, in a three-stage model proposed by Anderson, (1982; Tenison et al., 2016), the earliest declarative stage of skill acquisition is characterized by high working memory demands, as task-relevant information must be actively maintained and rehearsed.
text.formatted: For instance, in a three-stage model proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Anderson, (1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Tenison et al., 2016)</ref>, the earliest declarative stage of skill acquisition is characterized by high working memory demands, as task-relevant information must be actively maintained and rehearsed.

text.text: In contrast, later stages involve a progressive shift toward procedural, automatized performance with minimal working memory involvement.
Such findings suggest that deficits in working memory may not impair ISL itself, but rather delay or reduce the efficiency of automaticity.

Therefore, working memory could be targeted in cognitive training, possibly enhancing the active maintenance and rehearsal in declarative stage in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (Hinc et al., 2025; Kurtz et al., 2001).

text.text: In contrast, most studies which also measured explicit memory reported no correlation between ISL and explicit memory in patients (Hsieh et al., 2004; Marvel et al., 2005; Pedersen et al., 2008; Horan et al., 2008).

text.text: A possible explanation might be that long-term declarative memory, as assessed by instruments such as the WMS-R or HVLT, generally measures retrieval after a delay, a function different from how efficiently a person processes information while a task is actively underway.
Thus, whether a patient can accurately recall certain information seems to have no obvious association with how quickly an automatized response to a statistical regularity emerges in real time.

Altogether, our results point to diverse ISL performance in schizophrenia spectrum disorders shaped by task characteristics and specific symptom dimensions or domain-general cognitive abilities, rather than unified results across included studies.
The most promising moderators included task and stimulus type, although both will require further targeted evidence.
Disorganized symptomatology and working memory emerged as consistent correlates, with further evidence needed for the effects of clinical state or antipsychotic medication type.
On the other hand, antipsychotic dosage, overall symptomatology, illness duration and phase, and other explicit memory skills did not seem to consistently relate to ISL.
Further evidence remains needed to assess the extent to which the available findings generalize outside of the visual modality, or to tests such as the transitional probabilities task.
However, several limitations of the included studies limit the conclusions that can be drawn from this review.
First, sample sizes varied considerably, with some studies including as few as 10 patients (Hsieh et al., 2004; Reiss et al., 2006).

text.text: Moreover, the studies were mostly cross-sectional.

With the exception of Exner, Boucsein et al. (2006), which followed patients longitudinally across an acute episode and 20-month remission, no study assessed the same patients at more than one point in time.
text.formatted: With the exception of <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Exner, Boucsein et al. (2006)</ref>, which followed patients longitudinally across an acute episode and 20-month remission, no study assessed the same patients at more than one point in time.

text.text: Furthermore, reporting of clinical and demographic variables was inconsistent across studies.

Finally, the methodological quality of the included studies varied considerably, with the weaker studies showing shortcomings mainly in control selection and in adjustment for confounders such as age and sex.
As study quality was not used to weight or exclude studies, outcomes classified as preserved, impaired, or mixed ISL carry equal weight despite different risk of bias.
